messages.body_plain:
Dear lavaan-useres,
I am facing a "problem" concerning the estimation of the meanstructure in a cfa-model. I have a multigroup model (2 groups) for which I am intersted in
a) the latent means of the factors (and the mean differences between the two groups)
b) the means of the observed variables (and the mean differrences between the two groups)
I am using effects-coding. Everything works fine, scalar invariance holds, so I am using the model with scalar invariances restrictions to estimate the mean-differences between the groups via ":="-specification. For the latent factors this works well, but for the means/intercepts of the observed variables, the standard errors were so large that I wonder if this is normal. As a result, the obvious mean differences (with sometimes strong effects) are no longer significant.

Using the Holzinger-Swinford-data, it is the same with the high standard errors, even with single group-model, when estimating the meanstructure.

HS.model1 <- '
 visual =~ x1 + x2 + x3
 textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
 speed =~ x7 + x8 + x9

 #labeling the respective intercepts
 x2 ~ intcx2*1
 x3 ~ intcx3*1
 #difference

 '

summary(model1,fit.measures=TRUE, remove.unused = FALSE)

messages.subject_clean: Running SEM on imputed data
messages.body_plain:
I don't know why the semTools tarball wouldn't download.  Have you tried it again in a fresh R session?

Having semTools installed shouldn't be necessary just to use the lavaan.mi package.  Additionally having the latest semTools is only necessary if you want to use a non-deprecated function like compRelSEM() on the new lavaan.mi package's output.

> when running this model separately on all 20 datasets the indirect effect is significant for 19 out of the 20 datasets. So I was wondering why the indirect pooled effect is sig. when using my first model but not when using the latent model?

It is hard to keep track of what you are comparing, but you can't expect results to be the same modeling different data (e.g., a composite vs. a common factor with multiple indicators), nor can you expect pooled results to mimic each imputation's results.  Each slope might be significantly different from 0, but those estimates might vary so much across imputations that the pooled SE correctly reflects the additional uncertainty (the between-imputation variance component).

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

Dear Yago,

sorry for not being precise in my question and thank you for taking care of my question.
I generalize the question: My goal is to compare the latent factor means of my two groups. That works wonderfully. But now I would also like to carry out a group comparison at indicator level. For example, I have a factor with 4 indicators:
import =~ e1110 + e1120 + e1130 + e1140

I estimate the model and use the difference variable to output the group difference of the factor mean :
#labeling
avail ~ c(lm2.group1, lm2.group2)*1
#difference variable
dlm2 := lm2.group1 - lm2.group2 #avail

How can I realize in lavaan to output the group differences for the 4 indicators individually to see which of the indicators has the biggest/smallest difference? At the moment I do it like this:

 #labeling
 e1110 ~ c(lm10.group1, lm10.group2)*1
 e1120 ~ c(lm20.group1, lm20.group2)*1
 e1130 ~ c(lm30.group1, lm30.group2)*1

 dlm5 := lm20.group1 - lm20.group2
 dlm6 := lm30.group1 - lm30.group2
 dlm7 := lm40.group1 - lm40.group2

In the manifest world, I would simply do an unpaired Welch-test for the 4 indicators.
Do I have to build a model, in which I create 4 phantom variables (i. e.: Variable1 =~ e1110, Variable2 =~ e1120, ...) and treat them as factors?

In the example above, I was wondering, in general, why do the standard errors of the intercepts increase so much as soon as I estimate the mean value structure?

Kindly,
Marcus

Thanks, Marcus.

For the configural and metric invariance levels, I would do as you did.

#labeling e1110 ~ c(lm10.group1, lm10.group2)*1 e1120 ~ c(lm20.group1, lm20.group2)*1 e1130 ~ c(lm30.group1, lm30.group2)*1 e1140 ~ c(lm40.group1, lm40.group2)*1 #difference variables dlm4 := lm10.group1 - lm10.group2 dlm5 := lm20.group1 - lm20.group2 dlm6 := lm30.group1 - lm30.group2 dlm7 := lm40.group1 - lm40.group2

For higher levels of invariance, this syntax is troublesome because scalar invariance forces the intercepts to be equal for all groups. From my tests, you should remove the abovementioned labels or they will rewrite lavaan’s code and test a model with all intercepts freely estimated.

What you can do in this case is delete the labels and, after fitting the scalar invariant model (or one with stronger invariance), use function lavaan::lavTestScore to run uni- and multivariate chi-squared tests concerning the equality constraints.

Best,
Yago

Dear Yago,

Thank you for thinking along with me. I understand the assignment of labels and simultaneous invariance restrictions of the intercepts. I have now tried again: the standard errors of the intercepts of the indicator variables (not the latent means) are enormously high even without invariance restrictions, regardless of the assigned labels. I calculated the whole thing with effects-coding. If I calculate it with ULI, then the standard errors are in the normal range.

I think I have found a workaround: For the comparison of the indicator means, I now simply estimate a model in which I do not load the indicators onto the latent variable, but model each indicator as a "single indicator latent variable" ("pseudo-factors", cf. Brown, 2015, p. 122ff.) (with effects.coding). I then have the mean values of the indicators of the complete sample (since FIML is active and there are missings on some variables) and compare the indicator mean values in this model using difference variables.

cfa_2fac_crs5_mm <- '
#measurement model
e1110f =~ e1110
e1120f =~ e1120
e1130f =~ e1130
e1140f =~ e1140

#Labels
e1010f ~ c(m.e1010.group1, m.e1010.group2)*1
e1020f ~ c(m.e1020.group1, m.e1020.group2)*1
e1030f ~ c(m.e1030.group1, m.e1030.group2)*1
e1040f ~ c(m.e1040.group1, m.e1040.group2)*1

#difference variables
e1010f ~ c(m.e1010.group1, m.e1010.group2)*1
e1020f ~ c(m.e1020.group1, m.e1020.group2)*1
e1030f ~ c(m.e1030.group1, m.e1030.group2)*1
e1040f ~ c(m.e1040.group1, m.e1040.group2)*1
'

fitcfa_2fac_crs5_mm <- cfa(cfa_2fac_crs5_mm, data=data_sub, estimator="MLR", missing="fiml", meanstructure = TRUE, effect.coding = T, group = "t1a12")

summary(fitcfa_2fac_crs5_mm, standardized=TRUE, fit.measures = TRUE, rsquare = TRUE)

This works fine.

Don't know whether or not this is the right way doing it. My subsamples are not that big (group 1: 62, group 2: 93), so too me, the standard errors fro the comparisons seems ok now.

Kindly,
Marcus

If I remove this item from the model, lavaan can fit the data as expected. Any suggestions on how to address this error? Why might this be occurring? Thanks, Jonah

From there, I created ordered indicators based on pairs. That is, if item 1 is ranked ahead of item 2, the indicator i1i2 gets a 1, and zero otherwise.

ph =~ 0

  lambda21 == 1 - exp(-b2 * 2)
  lambda31 == 1 - exp(-b2 * 3)
  lambda41 == 1 - exp(-b2 * 4)

Instats is offering a 2-day workshop on Using ChatGPT and Copilot for Efficient Data Analysis in R <https://instats.org/seminar/using-chatgpt-and-copilot-for-data-analy2?utm_source=lavaan>, running August 29 - 30, by professor Peter Gruber (who holds dual PhDs in physics and economics). This workshop provides a 21st-century introduction to Statistical Analysis with R, focusing on the efficient use of AI assistants including ChatGPT and Github Copilot to automate R coding with plain language requests. Because R is free, this revolution will help democratize access to basic and advanced analysis tools without having to suffer the learning curve of coding in R, including for qualitative and mixed methods research. Participants will learn step by step how to install AI tools and how to harness their power for efficient data analysis in R, making them many times more efficient. They will be able to create R code in the blink of an eye and with unprecedented ease of use, while learning some of the underlying principles of the R language as this relates to competently assessing and using AI-generated code.

Professor Gruber also have two separate 2-day workshops on how to use ChatGPT's newly updated Advanced Data Analysis tool to natively analyze data using ChatGPT. These workshops are timed for the EU and US time zones, with the first one Using ChatGPT for Advanced Data Analysis 3.0 (EU) <https://instats.org/seminar/using-chatgpt-for-advanced-data-analysis10-1?utm_source=lavaan> on September 16 - 17, and the second Using ChatGPT for Advanced Data Analysis 3.0 (US) <https://instats.org/seminar/using-chatgpt-for-advanced-data-analysis10-2?utm_source=lavaan> on October 19 and 22.

> unable to find an inherited method for function ‘Summary’ for signature ‘"lavaan"’

Did you type "Summary"? It should be "summary", all lower case.

By the way, not related to lavaan but related to meta-analysis. Have you thought about using metaSEM to do the meta-analysis? I understood it was common to use harmonic mean or some other methods to get a "sample size" to do meta-analytic structural equation modeling (MASEM). However, other methdos, such as two-stage SEM, are theoretically more defensible in doing MASEM. For example, instead of trying to find a number ("sample size") to represent the sampling error, TSSEM directly estimates the sampling error:

This can be done by metaSEM:

https://cran.r-project.org/package=metaSEM

A lot of features have been added since 2015 but the following paper may still be good paper to give you an idea of the approach, using the package for illustration:

Cheung, M. W.-L. (2015). metaSEM: An R package for meta-analysis using structural equation modeling. Frontiers in Psychology, 5(January), 1–7. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2014.01521

Chapter 7 of the following book also introduces the TSSEM approach:

Cheung, M. W. L. (2015). Meta-analysis: A structural equation modeling approach. John Wiley & Sons, Inc.

Hope this helps.

-- Shu Fai

Thanks everyone for your help, especially Shu Fai. Your reply solved the problem.

Hi Shu Fai:

Thanks very much for your suggestions. I really like MASEM and I have the book you reference.  I also did Mike Cheung's  online, 3 day workshop this January which I highly recommend.

I also like the following two articles:

Jak, S. & Cheung, M. W-L. (2020). Meta-analytic structural equation modeling with moderating effects on SEM parameters. Psychological Methods, 25(4), 430–455. http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/met0000245

Jak, S., Li, H., Kolbe, L., de Jonge, H., & Cheung, MW-L. (2021). Meta‐analytic structural equation modeling made easy: A tutorial and web application for one‐stage MASEM. Research Synthesis Methods, 12(5), 590-606. https://doi.org/10.1002/jrsm.1498
I did do MASEM using the metaSEM package for the core theoretical model as the effects sizes (correlations) are based upon a relatively large number of studies.

However, some of the paths in the full theoretical model have not been studied very much and the effect sizes for some of these peripheral paths are only based upon a few studies.
When I try to to use metaSEM for the  full theoretical model, then the package cannot handle the large amount of missing data when estimating the peripheral paths (the solution is unstable). This is why I am using a univariate (old fashioned) approach and the harmonic mean to test the full theoretical model.

All the best,

Peter

hi,

I think the answer to this question is suggested in this thread
https://groups.google.com/g/lavaan/c/AKN2CnF6i5g/m/3E20fDFdGAAJ
but I would love to be sure.

For a simulation study, we need to simulate manifest scores based on factor scores with a given mean vector and variance-covariance matrix. We can do this "automatically" with simulateData (by specifying the model associating factor and manifest variables), or "manually" (with mvrnorm from MASS to simulate factor scores, then combine these, according to out model, with residuals simulated with rnorm). Whereas the manual approach lets us obtain both manifest and factor scores (by first simulating factor and residual scores, then combining these to obtain the manifest scores), it appears that the automatic approach with simulateData only produces the former (because it appears that this function does not simulate factor scores, but uses the model speicification to derive the implied moment matrix and eventually mean vector of the manifest variables and based on those then simulates directly the manifest scores).

If this is correct, it means that simulateData does not allow obtaining true factor scores.

Thus, if we need to have both manifest scores and their underlying true factor scores we cannot use simulateData but have to use a "manual" (traditional R) approach.

Correct?

many thanks,

Hi all,

I have an SEM model that uses the WLSMV estimator due to ordinal data in my data set. I'll paste the code below. After fitting, I'm trying to get the correlation residuals  with "lavaan::residuals(fit, type = "cor.bollen")" but the $cov.x matrix of non-latent variables contains all 0s.

$cov.x age20 Gender Ethnct PrtnrS ELSI_2 NumCC age20 0 Gender 0 0 Ethnicity 0 0 0 PartnerStatus 0 0 0 0 ELSI_est20 0 0 0 0 0 NumCC 0 0 0 0 0 0

I do get a matrix for the latent variables ($res.cov). I'm wondering if I'm doing something wrong, if this actually means something, or if it has to do with the WLSMV estimation method. When I use ML estimation, I get numbers in the matrix which leads me to believe it's something with WLSMV. My code for the model and fit is below. Thanks!

model.numcc <- '
  # Measurement
  CESD20 =~ HCESDa20 + HCESDb20 + HCESDc20 + HCESDd20 + HCESDe20r + HCESDf20 + HCESDg20 + HCESDh20r + HCESDj20
  CESD22 =~ HCESDa22 + HCESDb22 + HCESDc22 + HCESDd22 + HCESDe22r + HCESDf22 + HCESDg22 + HCESDh22r + HCESDj22
  ELONE =~ FLONEi20 + FLONEj20 + FLONEc20
  SLONE =~ FLONEd20r + FLONEg20r + FLONEh20r

  # Structural
  ELONE ~ age20 + Gender + Ethnicity + PartnerStatus + ELSI_est20 + el_num*NumCC + CESD20
  SLONE ~ age20 + Gender + Ethnicity + PartnerStatus + ELSI_est20 + sl_num*NumCC + CESD20
  CESD22 ~ age20 + Gender + Ethnicity + PartnerStatus + ELSI_est20 + d22_num*NumCC + d22_sl*SLONE + d22_el*ELONE + CESD20

  # Direct effect
  dir_numcc := d22_num

  # Indirect effects
  ind_sl := sl_num*d22_sl
  ind_el := el_num*d22_el
  tot_ind := ind_sl + ind_el

  # Total effect
  tot := dir_numcc + tot_ind

  # Covariances
  ELONE ~~ SLONE
  '

fit <- sem(model.numcc, data = data_final, estimator="WLSMV", ordered=TRUE, parallel = "multicore")

Tom
